Female Coolie loaches attain an ultimate total length of 12 centimeters [Li = 12 centimeters], a modest size typical of the genus Pangio, which encompasses small, eel-like bottom dwellers native to Southeast Asian streams. Field surveys in peat swamp forests of Borneo have recorded individuals approaching this asymptotic length, though most adults encountered are somewhat smaller, likely due to food limitation and the energetic demands of burrowing through soft substrates. The maximum body mass corresponding to this length in females has been estimated at 10.3 grams [Wwi = 10.3 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions applied to a museum series of gravid specimens. This relatively low mass reflects the species' elongate, serpentiform body plan, which minimises the allometric increase in weight with length, a common feature among cobitid loaches that navigate interstitial spaces within leaf litter and sediment.

Sexual maturation in female Pangio kuhlii occurs at a markedly smaller size than the ultimate adult length, with individuals first attaining reproductive capability at a total length of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters]. At this developmental milestone, corresponding to the onset of vitellogenesis and the first visible enlargement of the ovary, body mass averages approximately 2.0 grams [Wwp = approximately 2.0 grams]. The transition from juvenile to mature state is thus accompanied by a nearly fivefold increase in wet weight before the fish reaches its final adult dimensions, a pattern consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritises early reproductive output over continued rapid somatic expansion. Histological examination of gonadal tissues from wild-caught specimens confirms that oocyte development becomes active once the 7 centimeter threshold is crossed.

The egg of the Coolie loach is small and yolk-laden, typical of demersal spawners that deposit adhesive clutches among fine-leaved aquatic vegetation. Based on an observed oocyte diameter of one millimetre, the wet weight of a newly fertilised ovum at birth is calculated at 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams]. This extremely low birth mass, equivalent to roughly half a milligram, is consistent with the production of numerous small eggs, a fecundity strategy that compensates for high rates of larval mortality in unpredictable floodplain environments. The yolk reserves contained within this minute chorion sustain the prolarva through its endotrophic phase, during which mouthparts develop and the yolk sac is progressively resorbed, before the onset of exogenous feeding on rotifers and ciliates.

Longevity records for Pangio kuhlii based on captive maintenance at a stable water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] indicate that individuals can survive for approximately 5110 days [am = approximately 5110 days], equivalent to roughly fourteen years, before succumbing to senescence. This extended lifespan is notable for a fish of such diminutive size and likely reflects a slow metabolic pace associated with life in cool, oxygen-poor, acidic blackwater habitats where foraging opportunities are sporadic and predation pressure from visual hunters is reduced by the turbid, stained water column. Age estimates derived from otolith microincrement counts in wild populations broadly corroborate the captive data, although mortality from environmental stressors typically truncates realised longevity in nature to a fraction of this physiological potential.

Under the same thermal regime of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] that yields maximal longevity, female Coolie loaches initiate spawning after reaching puberty, producing multiple clutches across an extended reproductive season. Individual spawnings consist of approximately thirty to fifty adhesive eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately thirty to fifty adhesive eggs per clutch], with gravid females depositing eggs on submerged leaf surfaces or among the fine roots of floating plants. The interval between successive spawning events in captivity has been recorded as roughly one clutch every three weeks [F_R_i = roughly one clutch every three weeks], a frequency that, when combined with clutch size, yields a substantial cumulative annual reproductive output for a fish weighing at maturity only 2.0 grams [Wwp = 2.0 grams]. This iteroparous strategy allows the species to buffer against variable juvenile survival in its dynamic floodplain nursery habitats.
